subject: physics
question_text: A pump is required to lift 600 kg of water per minute from a well of 25 m deep and to eject it with a speed of 50 ms⁻¹. Calculate the power required to perform the above task. (g = 10 ms⁻²)

verification.note: Printed as the applied half of an 8-mark Section-C question in TS March 2016 (Q19) and TS March 2020 (Q19), Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I. The 4-mark standalone length is our authoring choice, not the board's — the board never printed it as a 4-mark Section-B question. Unlike ts_ipe_p1_wpe_pump_power_lift_only, this question gives an ejection speed, so the ½mv² term is required and is the point of the card. Arithmetic hand-checked with the printed g = 10 m s⁻²: 600/60 = 10 kg s⁻¹; mgh/t = 10 × 10 × 25 = 2500 W; ½mv²/t = ½ × 10 × (50)² = ½ × 10 × 2500 = 12500 W; total = 15000 W = 15 kW. A published guide prints 14.95 kW because it uses g = 9.8 m s⁻² for the potential term; the paper prints g = 10, so 15 kW is written here and the 14.95 kW discrepancy is recorded rather than silently followed or silently corrected. The three-way split is invented and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The rate in kg s⁻¹
lines: Convert the rate first. The pump handles
That same 10 kg is raised through 25 m and
steps.margin_note: First mark. One conversion line, and it is used twice later.
steps.why: The same 10 kg s⁻¹ does two jobs in this question: it is raised through the depth and it leaves the pipe with speed. Fixing the rate first lets both energy terms be written per second, which is what a power answer needs.
common_mistakes: Using 600 kg as the mass handled in one second.
Converting the rate and then using the converted value in only one of the two terms.

recall.must_convey: That 600 kg per minute is 10 kg per second, and that same 10 kg is both raised and ejected.
accept: the same ten kg is lifted and ejected

steps.memory_tip: 10 kg every second, and that same 10 kg is both raised and ejected.

steps.label: Two energy terms
lines: The water is raised through h = 25 m and
also leaves at v = 50 ms⁻¹, so the pump
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The added ½mv² term is the whole point of this question.
steps.why: This is the one difference from a pump that only lifts. Water that is only raised arrives at the top with no speed, so mgh is the entire cost. Here the water leaves at 50 ms⁻¹, and that kinetic energy came from the pump too, so ½mv² is added to the potential term.
common_mistakes: Dropping the ½mv² term and answering 2500 W, which is the lifting cost alone.
Using m = 600 kg in the kinetic term instead of the 10 kg handled in one second.

recall.must_convey: That the power is m g h plus half m v squared, all divided by t — both terms, not just the lifting one.
accept: m g h plus half m v squared by t
the ejection speed adds a kinetic term
reject: only m g h by t
heard_as: mgh plus half m v squared

steps.memory_tip: Raised and thrown means two terms: mgh for the height, ½mv² for the speed.

steps.label: The power
lines: The paper prints g = 10 m s⁻². Substitute
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. Both terms shown, then one boxed total with its unit.
steps.why: The paper prints g = 10 m s⁻², so 15 kW is the marked answer. A published guide gives 14.95 kW because it uses g = 9.8 m s⁻² for the potential term; that gap of 50 W comes only from the value of g, not from any difference in the physics. Use the value the paper prints.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 2500 W, the lifting term alone.
Using 600 kg in the kinetic term, which makes that term 60 times too large.

recall.must_convey: That the two terms are 2500 W and 12500 W, so P = 15000 W = 15 kW.
accept: two thousand five hundred plus twelve thousand five hundred
reject: two thousand five hundred watt only

steps.memory_tip: 2500 W to raise it, 12500 W to eject it: 15000 W in all, which is 15 kW.

insider_note: The kinetic term is 12500 of the 15000 W, so an answer that stops at 2500 W keeps the first two marks and loses the last two.
